people.label: David Charles Grusch
people.sub: USAF Maj (ret.); NGA GS-15; NRO rep to UAP Task Force 2019-2021
people.narrative: Grusch is the hinge of the modern disclosure record: the first person holding a current TS//SCI clearance with CI and lifestyle polygraph and a UAP Task Force billet to state under oath that the United States runs a multi-decade UAP crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering effort concealed from Congress. His resume is documentary, not anecdotal. The House Oversight Committee published his biography: intelligence officer 2009-2023; 21st Operations Group Space Control Intelligence Cell; 3d Space Experimentation Squadron; Chief, Intelligence Integration Division, Space Security and Defense Program 2013-2016; Senior Intelligence Officer at the National Reconnaissance Office 2016-2021 on the Director's briefing staff coordinating the President's Daily Brief; then GS-15 Senior GEOINT Capabilities Requirements Officer at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency from November 2021 to April 2023. He was NRO's representative to the UAP Task Force 2019-2021 and NGA's co-lead for UAP and trans-medium object analysis from late 2021 into 2022. He testified that in 2019 the UAP Task Force Director tasked him to identify every special access program and controlled access program needed to satisfy the Task Force's congressionally mandated mission; that he was then informed in the course of official duties of a multi-decade crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering program; and that he was denied the read-ons when he requested them. That denial - a cleared officer legally tasked to inventory SAPs being refused - is the structural fact this board turns on. He disclosed to the DoD Inspector General in July 2021 and filed a PPD-19 urgent-concern complaint with the Intelligence Community Inspector General on 25 May 2022 through counsel Charles McCullough III, the IC's first Inspector General; ICIG found it credible and urgent in July 2022. DoD's own Prepublication and Security Review cleared his statements for open publication on 4 and 6 April 2023 - the Pentagon's security apparatus signed off on the words the Pentagon's press office later called unsubstantiated. He went public through Leslie Kean and Ralph Blumenthal in The Debrief on 5 June 2023, on NewsNation with Ross Coulthart days later, and under oath before House Oversight on 26 July 2023, where he stated he had interviewed over 40 witnesses over four years, that biologics came with some recoveries and were nonhuman, that he has personal knowledge of people harmed in the concealment effort, and that the programs run on misappropriation of funds and contractor IR&D self-funding. Eli Crane's 24 July 2025 letter to DoD - and the FOIA leak of his 2014 and 2018 emergency-custody police records to The Intercept in August 2023, which he litigated and lost. Since 27 March 2025 he has been Special Advisor to Rep. Eric Burlison and a fixture of the House Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets, appearing at the 9 June 2026 Capitol press conference where he alleged slush funds of billions of dollars per annum and said the government is aware of several kinds of non-human intelligence.

grusch-icig-complaint.desc: Chain of custody for the complaint, as established by sworn testimony and reporting. July 2021: Grusch makes a protected disclosure of classified information to the DoD Inspector General concerning the improper withholding and concealment of UAP-related material from Congress. 25 May 2022: Irvin Charles McCullough III of Compass Rose Legal Group, the first Inspector General of the Intelligence Community, files a PPD-19 urgent-concern complaint with the ICIG on Grusch's behalf. July 2022: the ICIG determines the complaint credible and urgent, the statutory trigger for transmission to the congressional intelligence committees. A companion reprisal complaint alleges Grusch's identity and his DoD IG communications were disclosed to DoD and IC entities outside the IG's office; the unclassified version reported in June 2023 references DNI Avril Haines, AARO director Sean Kirkpatrick, DoD spokesperson Susan Gough, Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand and Rep. Tim Burchett in its account of how the information moved. Grusch's unclassified description of the underlying subject matter, given under oath to Chairman Grothman: 'Both material acquisition and exploitation activity, also baselining the UAPs but not sharing it with, you know, intelligence professionals that are actually doing step briefs to pilots.' He further testified that the preponderance of the complaint was classified, that he knows the exact locations of held material and provided them to the Inspector General and in part to the intelligence committees, and that he had the individuals with firsthand knowledge make their own protected disclosures. He also testified to a routing failure: PPD-19 and ICD 120 send such disclosures to the intelligence committees, and there was no good mechanism for the ICIG to provide his information to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees despite Title 10 equities being at play.

gaps: The program name. Grusch was formally tasked to inventory all SAPs and CAPs bearing on a congressionally mandated mission and was refused a read-on. The refusing authority, the program nickname, and the refusal document have never been identified. The DoD Special Access Program Central Office under Maj. Gen. David W. Abba is the office that would hold that record; no committee has publicly compelled it.

The witness list. Under oath on 26 July 2023 Grusch offered Rep. Nancy Mace 'a specific cooperative and hostile witness list of specific individuals' and said he would provide it after the hearing. Three years later there is no public evidence the list was received, retained, or acted on. Locating it - via committee records request or a member's office - is the single highest-yield next step in this domain.

The roughly 40 witnesses. Grusch swore he had the firsthand-knowledge individuals file their own protected disclosures with the Inspector General. Whether the ICIG adjudicated any of them, and whether AARO ever interviewed any of them, is unknown. AARO's assertion that none of its interviewees had firsthand knowledge is consistent with AARO simply never having reached that pool.

The DOPSR file. DoD holds the full text of the answers Grusch submitted for prepublication review in March and April 2023, withheld from the 23-F-0946 release under FOIA exemption (b)(6). The Black Vault has appealed. Those answers are the closest thing to a written deposition Grusch has ever given, and they sit in a government file.

The reprisal paper trail. Rep. Eli Crane's 24 July 2025 letter enumerates three specific administrative actions - clearance revocation, promotion denial, and loss of medical retirement. Each generates internal DoD documentation with dates, adjudicators and stated grounds. None has been produced, and DoD did not reply to the letter on the record.

The 'events in recent days.' George Knapp told the Task Force on 9 September 2025 that extra-legal reprisals against Grusch had occurred in the days before the hearing. No member asked what he meant; no reporting has identified the events.

The reprisal complaint's disposition. The unclassified version reported in June 2023 alleges Grusch's identity and his DoD IG communications leaked outside the protected channel. The ICIG's finding on that complaint - whether substantiated, unsubstantiated, or still open - has never been made public.

The identity of 'Jonathan Grey.' A serving NASIC officer at Wright-Patterson corroborated on the record under a pseudonym. Whether NASIC took action against him, and whether he was among the 40 witnesses, is unknown.

AARO's underlying interviews. The Historical Record Report's central impeachment - that none of the interviewees had firsthand knowledge - rests on an interview set AARO has never published, listed, or characterized by count or seniority. The claim cannot be audited.

The April 2022 Kirkpatrick meeting. Grusch swore he briefed Kirkpatrick in a classified setting three months before Kirkpatrick led AARO. Kirkpatrick has never publicly denied it and never explained why it did not generate a line of inquiry. Any contemporaneous memorandum of that conversation would be dispositive on what AARO knew and when.

The Title 10 routing failure. Grusch testified the ICIG had no smooth mechanism to send his disclosure to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees despite Title 10 equities. Whether those committees ever received the substance is unresolved, and no subsequent statute has visibly closed the gap.

The IR&D trail. Grusch's sworn funding mechanism - misappropriation plus contractor internal research and development money outside the notification architecture - is testable against DCAA audit records, FPDS and USAspending contract data, and Periodic Program Review documentation. No public work has yet attempted that reconciliation.

The 2026 releases. The February 2026 declassification announcement and the July 2026 NDA waiver directive are both process commitments without deadlines. What has actually been transferred to the National Archives UAP Collection since April 2025, and whether anything responsive to Grusch's allegations appears in it, is the measurable that will settle much of this domain.
